title: A lamp where no wind blows
hookLine: a clay lamp on a windowsill lies flat when the door opens, and stands up again when it shuts
carry: abhyasa and vairagya: practice, and letting go

lines: A CLAY LAMP ON A WINDOWSILL.
THE DOOR OPENS. THE FLAME LIES DOWN.
THE DOOR SHUTS. IT STANDS UP.
cards: A small clay lamp sits on a windowsill, a cotton wick in a pool of oil. Someone opens the front door. A version runs through the house, and the flame lies down sideways, thin and blue, nearly out.
The door shuts. For a moment the flame shivers. Then it stands back up, tall and still, as if nothing happened.
A small drama, easy to miss. The Bhagavad Gita uses that same flame to describe a mind.

teach.h: A LAMP WHERE NO WIND BLOWS.
teach.b: In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna describes someone sitting in meditation, and then gives a single picture.
In paraphrase: as a lamp in a place without wind does not flicker, so is the mind of the yogi who has gathered it in.

Kalidasa, in yesterday's story, paints the meditating Shiva the same way: like a lamp unmoving where no wind blows. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the yogi has no mind, or that the flame goes out.
The lamp is still burning, still giving light. What's gone is the flicker. Arjuna, listening, isn't convinced.

teach.h: ARJUNA: AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.
teach.b: A few verses later he pushes back: the mind is restless, Krishna, stubborn and strong, and holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It's an honest complaint, and the text keeps it in. Krishna doesn't argue.
He agrees the mind is hard to hold.

teach.h: ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA: PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.
teach.b: Then he names two things that hold it: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go. Practice is coming back, again and again. Letting go is not feeding every version that blows through.

teach.h: WHEREVER IT WANDERS, DRAW IT BACK.
teach.b: Earlier in the same chapter, Krishna puts the coming back in plain terms: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there, and rest it again in the Self.

teach.h: THE FLAME STILL BURNS. ONLY THE FLICKER GOES.
teach.b: That's why the flame suits trataka so well. The eyes rest on the very thing the Gita compares the mind to. The practice is simply to notice when attention leans, like a flame in a version, and come back.
The Gita never promises the wind will stop forever. It describes a lamp in a sheltered place, and a person who keeps coming back to it.

how: Some who practice trataka use a candle or ghee lamp set at eye level in a still, version-free room, and some recall the Gita's image of a lamp in a windless place as they sit.

o: a still gaze on one point, returning when you drift
a lamp kept lit all night where no wind can reach
watching a flame until your thoughts stop for good

games.q: the Gita's lamp — tap the pairs.
p: a lamp in a windless place
the mind of the yogi, gathered in
as hard as holding the wind

s: in the Gita's image, the steady mind is a flame that has gone out
the lamp is still burning and giving light; only the flicker is gone.
Arjuna tells Krishna the mind is as hard to hold as the wind
he says so in chapter six, and Krishna agrees it is hard to hold.
Krishna promises the mind's wind will stop forever
he names practice and letting go, and says to draw the mind back wherever it wanders.

games.q: you're Krishna. Arjuna says holding the mind is as hard as holding the wind. what do you answer?
o: he's wrong; it's easy once you try.
he's right, and practice and letting go will hold it.
he's right, so it can't be done.
games.why: Krishna agrees the mind is restless and hard to hold, then names abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go.

practice: Set a candle flame safely lit, or a mark on the wall, at eye level, and let the eyes rest on it, blinking whenever you need to.

Each time a sound, a plan or a memory pulls you away, notice the lean, like a flame in a version, and come back to the point: no scolding, just return. If the eyes tire, close them for a while, then open them and look again.

wordCard.voice: Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, with the Gita's lamp in a windless place, and the coming back each time the mind leans.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: abhyasa, practice, the returning again and again. In the Gita, paired with vairagya, letting go.

carryVoice: Your line: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go. The flame still burns; only the flicker goes. See you tomorrow.
